name: MarCO A and B
short_status: In orbit around the Sun and silent since 4 January 2019. The two CubeSats relayed InSight's landing live from about 3,500 km out on 26 November 2018, then stopped answering within six weeks.
tagline: NASA · United States · Flyby · 2018 · The long occupation Success
stats: CubeSats to fly to deep space, on NASA's own account
one-way light time their live relay of the landing had to cross

facts.label: What they were
facts.value: Two identical six-unit CubeSats, officially MarCO-A and MarCO-B. NASA's landing press kit names them 'MarCO-A and MarCO-B, also nicknamed EVE and Wall-E', in that order, after the two robots in the Pixar film. Each measured about 36.6 by 24.3 by 11.8 cm stowed and weighed 13.5 kg, with deployable solar arrays and antennas.

facts.label: Catalogue numbers
facts.value: MarCO-A is 2018-042B and MarCO-B is 2018-042C in NASA's NSSDCA master catalogue. Both launched with InSight, which is 2018-042A.

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 5 May 2018 at 11:05 UTC on the Atlas V 401 that carried InSight, from Vandenberg. Both were heard from the same day, at 12:15 p.m. and 1:58 p.m. PST, confirming their solar panels had deployed and their radios were alive. Chief engineer Andy Klesh: 'Both MarCO-A and B say Polo!'

facts.label: Radios
facts.value: A UHF antenna to receive InSight's transmissions during entry, a flat X-band high-gain reflect array to send them onward to Earth, and two smaller X-band antennas, low-gain and medium-gain. The relay ran at 8 kilobits per second.

facts.label: Propulsion
facts.value: Eight thrusters using compressed R236FA, described by NASA as a common propellant in fire extinguishers. They made the first trajectory correction manoeuvres ever performed by CubeSats, each steering itself toward Mars.

facts.label: The leak
facts.value: MarCO-B, the one nicknamed Wall-E, leaked propellant almost from liftoff. Andy Klesh, four days before the landing: 'WALL-E has been leaking fuel almost since liftoff.' Of the other he said 'EVE seems to follow her namesake and has been flying beautifully throughout the [mission].' Controllers worked around the leak and MarCO-B still made its flyby and its relay.

facts.label: The firsts NASA claims
facts.value: NASA's landing press kit says MarCO 'is the first deep space mission for CubeSats', that the pair 'became the first CubeSats to fly to deep space', and that they were 'the first CubeSats to provide images of Earth, its moon and Mars'. These are NASA's formulations and we have not independently audited every one of them.

facts.label: First picture of Mars from a CubeSat
facts.value: Taken on 3 October 2018 by the wide-angle camera on top of MarCO-B as a test of exposure settings, from roughly 12.8 million km out, with parts of the high-gain antenna visible on either side of the frame. NASA released it on 22 October 2018.

facts.label: What they did on landing day
facts.value: Each flew past Mars about 3,500 km away as InSight entered the atmosphere, receiving InSight's UHF stream, reformatting it and sending it Earthward across about 146 million km, a trip of 8 minutes and 7 seconds at the speed of light. That is why the landing could be followed almost live rather than reconstructed afterwards from a recording.

facts.label: Whether it worked
facts.value: It did. The abstract of Andrew Klesh's flight-results paper, filed with NASA's technical reports server on 21 October 2019, states that 'the MarCO spacecraft successfully flew by Mars while relaying entry-descent-and-landing telemetry for the InSight vehicle' and that both craft 'performed beyond expectations and were able to provide a realtime link for the so-called seven minutes of terror'.

facts.label: InSight did not depend on them
facts.value: NASA said so before the fact. The landing press kit states that 'InSight's success is independent of its CubeSat tag-alongs' and that Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and 2001 Mars Odyssey held primary telecommunications responsibility for the landing. MarCO shortened the wait for news; it was not the only way the news could arrive.

facts.label: The flyby picture, and a NASA arithmetic slip
facts.value: MarCO-B photographed Mars during the flyby on 26 November 2018. NASA's two current pages disagree on how far away it was: the JPL mission page says 'about 4,700 miles (7,600 kilometers)' and NASA Science's MarCO page says 'about 4,700 miles (6,000 kilometers)'. 4,700 miles is 7,564 km, so the metric figure on the NASA Science page is a bad conversion of the same distance.

facts.label: Last contact
facts.value: MarCO-B on 29 December 2018 and MarCO-A on 4 January 2019, as listed in NASA's own key dates for the mission. That is roughly a month and six weeks after the flyby respectively.

facts.label: The attempt to get them back
facts.value: English Wikipedia records a NASA campaign in September 2019 to re-establish contact once the geometry improved, and states that on 2 February 2020 NASA announced the mission had formally ended. The underlying report it cites is a Space.com article we could not open on 23 August 2026, so we present this as Wikipedia's account rather than as a NASA statement we have read. NASA's own MarCO page lists no event after 4 January 2019.

facts.label: Where they are now
facts.value: In orbit around the Sun, past Mars, silent. They were on flyby trajectories and never had the propulsion to enter Mars orbit, so they carried straight on. Nothing consulted on 23 August 2026 records a signal from either since 4 January 2019.

facts.label: Cost and team
facts.value: 18.5 million dollars, built and managed by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Joel Krajewski was project manager and Andrew Klesh project engineer and chief engineer.

timeline: Launch at 11:05 UTC on InSight's Atlas V 401 from Vandenberg. Both CubeSats report in the same afternoon, at 12:15 and 1:58 p.m. PST, with solar panels deployed and radios working.
MarCO-B's wide-angle camera takes the first picture of Mars from a CubeSat on 3 October, from about 12.8 million km, as a test of exposure settings. NASA releases it on 22 October.
Four days out, JPL confirms publicly that MarCO-B has been leaking propellant almost since liftoff, and that controllers have worked around it. Its twin is reported to be flying beautifully.
Both CubeSats fly past Mars about 3,500 km away, catch InSight's UHF signal through the entry and landing, and pass it to Earth across 146 million km, a light trip of 8 minutes and 7 seconds.
11:52 a.m. PST (19:52 UTC): touchdown confirmation reaches JPL by way of the two CubeSats. MarCO-B also photographs Mars during the flyby.
Last contact with MarCO-B, the leaky one, about a month after the flyby.
Last contact with MarCO-A. Nothing has been heard from either since.

NASA runs a campaign to re-establish contact as the two drift into a more favourable position relative to the Sun and Earth. Nothing answers. This account comes from English Wikipedia rather than from a NASA release we have read.
Andrew Klesh files the flight-results paper with NASA's technical reports server, recording that both spacecraft performed beyond expectations and provided a real-time link through the landing.
English Wikipedia records NASA announcing that the Mars Cube One mission has formally ended. NASA's own MarCO page carries no event after 4 January 2019.

NASA's MarCO mission page still lists 29 December 2018 and 4 January 2019 as the last contacts and describes the mission in the past tense. No source consulted today records any signal from either spacecraft since.

images.caption: Engineer Joel Steinkraus with both MarCO spacecraft at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in March 2018. The unit on the left is folded as it flew stowed on the rocket; the one on the right has its solar panels out, with its flat reflectarray high-gain antenna standing up behind it.

Mars photographed by MarCO-B's wide-angle camera on 26 November 2018 as the CubeSat flew away after InSight landed, with the grid of its reflectarray antenna along the right edge of the frame. The picture sits letterboxed inside a 1920 by 1080 canvas.

NASA's annotated version of MarCO-B's wide-angle camera view, taken as a test of exposure settings on 2 October 2018. Mars is the small red dot right of centre, ringed with a dashed circle and labelled by NASA; parts of the CubeSat's unfolded high-gain antenna show on both sides of the frame.
The first image returned by MarCO-B after launch, showing its unfolded high-gain antenna at right and Earth with the Moon as two points of light near the centre.
